item.title: PDO Drug Screening Data for Evaluating and Training AI Drug Response Prediction Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.15769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anti-cancer drug response prediction (DRP) is critically important for precision oncology and therapeutic development. Currently, most DRP models are developed using drug screening data from immortalized cancer cell lines, which can differ substantially from patient tumors at the genomic and molecular levels, even though patient tumor response is the ultimate prediction target. To help bridge this gap and bring DRP models closer to their intended clinical application, we conducted four drug screening studies using patient-derived organoids (PDOs), which more faithfully recapitulate patient tumors than immortalized cell lines. These studies generated data for improving and evaluating DRP models, including multi-omics profiles of PDO lines, drug feature data, and treatment response measurements. Using these data, we retrained and evaluated multiple publicly available DRP models under three model-building scenarios: training models using cell line data only, training models using combined cell line and PDO data, and pretraining models on cell line data followed by fine-tuning on PDO data. We then evaluated and compared model prediction performance on PDOs across these analysis scenarios. In addition, we also assessed the consistency of drug screening viability data generated by different laboratories using different assay technologies and/or experimental protocols.
item.dc:creator: Y. Zhu, K. Marlor, V. Lavelle, T. S. Brettin, M. Sacco, C. Siniscalchi, H. W. Raeder, M. R. Weil, R. L. Stevens

item.title: A risk-aware individualized blood pressure target to avoid hypotension in surgery
item.description: arXiv:2611.16757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an online method for choosing both a blood pressure target and a norepinephrine dose for an individual surgical patient. From a short record of mean arterial pressure (MAP) and norepinephrine delivery, the method fits a reduced pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic model and uses a local Gaussian approximation to propagate uncertainty to future MAP readings. It searches for the lowest target for which a bolus and constant infusion keep the predicted probability of at least one MAP reading below 65 mmHg after the rise phase within a prescribed limit. If no such target is found, the decision returns to the clinician. We assess calibration of the predicted minimum MAP on retrospective surgical records under the doses actually administered. In a cohort of 4,096 virtual patients, the method recommended a dose for 74 % of patients at a nominal risk of 5 %. Among the patients receiving a recommendation, 6.9 % had a reading below 65 mmHg. A fixed target of 70 mmHg yielded a rate of 25 % when applied to the full virtual cohort.
item.dc:creator: Simon Bur{\'e}, Jona Joachim, Florent Di Meglio

item.title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.16881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.
item.dc:creator: Paarth Batra, Aryan Keluskar

item.title: Robot-Induced Bias in Movement Smoothness Metrics for Rehabilitation: Quantification and Correction in Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.15743v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robot mechanics can bias kinematic measures of recovery and limit comparisons across rehabilitation devices. We developed a closed-loop human-robot simulation calibrated to published healthy and stroke group kinematics. Paired runs held motor-control parameters and movement plans fixed to quantify bias in seven metrics relative to a low-impedance reference, normalized using external repeatability benchmarks. Within a subset informed by published device specifications, median log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) bias was 0.93 and 1.79 benchmark units for stroke and healthy profiles, respectively. Sobol analysis identified Coulomb friction and apparent mass as leading contributors; LDLJ bias persisted across 11 robustness variants. LDLJ bias increased as simulated movements became less fragmented. If recovery similarly reduces fragmentation, this effect could partly mask improvement in measured smoothness. Correction combining identified robot dynamics and observed metrics with gradient-boosted trees reduced median normalized absolute error from 0.77 to 0.10 for LDLJ and from 0.24 to 0.08 for spectral arc length (SPARC) in the device-informed subset of a random 20% hold-out. Median smoothness residuals remained at or below 0.15 benchmark units across four separately held-out parameter regions. Under an alternative controller, LDLJ error decreased from 1.60 to 0.17 without retraining, although transfer varied across metrics. These simulation results support mechanical characterization and movement-dependent correction toward more comparable robotic assessments, motivating validation in patients.
item.dc:creator: David Regev, Alex Scherbakov, Eran Beeri Bamani

item.title: Silscore: modelling siRNA potency with positional thermodynamics and data-selected nucleotide-identity terms
item.description: arXiv:2611.15812v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) enable programmable gene silencing, but candidates targeting the same transcript can differ markedly in potency. Existing predictors range from interpretable empirical rules with limited accuracy to high-capacity models that can lose performance when datasets or targets change. We present Silscore, a guide-only model that combines a quadratic preference for overall duplex stability, a position-resolved profile of nearest-neighbour stacking energies and sparse nucleotide-identity terms selected from residuals left unexplained by thermodynamics. Its main fit uses 26 parameters, fewer than half as many as any trainable comparator evaluated here. We evaluate Silscore on the canonical split of the Huesken dataset, two external datasets (Mixset and Katoh-Suzuki), and an evaluation in which the same guides are tested after training on dissimilar targets. Silscore attains the highest observed Pearson correlation in all three transfer evaluations, and the data support an advantage over every applicable comparator on Katoh-Suzuki. For a fixed evaluation set, we compare two equally sized training sets with higher or lower sequence similarity to the evaluation sequences. After training on the less similar sequences, Silscore has the highest observed correlation, and the data do not establish a change in its performance. The fitted parameters can also be interpreted directly: identity terms locate sequence effects that base-pairing energies cannot express, global stability has a data-estimated intermediate optimum, and local energy profiles recover terminal asymmetry and a preference for weaker seed and stronger central pairing. Silscore thus provides a compact, data-driven model that combines strong predictive performance with robustness when tested in new settings and expresses previously reported empirical preferences as quantities estimated from data.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Sacco, Isabella Baldini, Riccardo Paone, Mattia Capulli, Guido Sanguinetti, Giovanni Bussi

item.title: Subject-Held-Out Evaluation of Deep Ground Reaction Force Estimators Across Two Laboratories: Leakage and Cross-Laboratory Transfer
item.description: arXiv:2611.15966v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep networks that estimate ground reaction forces and centers of pressure from motion-capture markers are validated within one laboratory, in a seldom-stated coordinate frame, and sometimes with trial-level splits that put the same person in the training and the test set. We measured what each practice costs, and whether such models transfer between laboratories. Three sequence models (convolutional, convolutional-recurrent, and convolutional-transformer) were evaluated on two independent datasets, locomotion (6 subjects) and occupational patient handling (10 subjects), under one pipeline, one tuning procedure, three seeds, and four protocols: trial-level split, leave-one-subject-out, pooled two-laboratory training with matched held-out subjects, and cross-laboratory transfer. At a fixed configuration, trial-level splits overstated the subject-held-out coefficient of determination by +0.040 to +0.194; on occupational data the overstatement exceeded every difference between architectures. With subjects held out, the three models reached values between 0.583 and 0.804; the leader differed between datasets, and gaps lay within subject-to-subject variability. Pooling the laboratories changed neither dataset on matched subjects. Transfer between laboratories was below chance in both directions, including the vertical force, which no in-plane rotation can affect. Leaving force targets in the plate frame while inputs were heading-aligned cost 0.57 of locomotion anteroposterior-force explained variance, enough to make that force look hardest; a Newton's-law correlation detected the mismatch before training. Split protocol and target frame changed reported accuracy more than architecture did. Learned force estimators should be validated with subjects held out, checked for frame consistency before training, and tested across laboratories before deployment claims are made.
item.dc:creator: Hernan David Santos, Yinong Chen, Yu Ding, Xudong Zhang, Jian Tao

item.title: Trajectory Inference of Human Aging from Cross-Sectional DNA Methylation Data
item.description: arXiv:2607.06583v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: DNA methylation (DNAm) serves as one of the most robust molecular biomarkers of biological aging. While conventional epigenetic clocks accurately predict chronological age from high-dimensional CpG profiles, they treat aging as a static regression task, meaning they can only output a single score rather than simulating how an entire profile continuously changes over time. To reconstruct these continuous dynamics, we frame lifelong human epigenetic aging as a trajectory inference problem across discrete age snapshots derived from widely available cross-sectional data. We introduce a two-stage computational pipeline: first, an age-regularized Variational Autoencoder (VAE) maps high-dimensional CpG profiles onto a chronologically ordered latent manifold while preserving a generative decoder bridge back to the original methylation space. Second, we model the continuous movement across this latent space via Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport (RUOT) that unifies deterministic drift, random diffusion, and non-conservative mass changes. By resolving this RUOT formulation using the DeepRUOT framework, our model fluidly accommodates population-level density shifts like survivorship bias and cellular attrition without requiring rigid biological priors. Evaluated on a large-scale, 80-year pan-tissue dataset, our model demonstrates robust distribution interpolation and uncovers a prominent late-life surge in the learned growth field that mathematically captures the variance expansion driven by stochastic epigenetic drift. Finally, by decoding continuous latent paths back to individual CpG sites, we reconstruct and empirically verify distinct biological aging archetypes, offering a rigorous, generative paradigm for simulating human molecular aging.
item.dc:creator: Chandan Gupta, Syed Haider, Pietro Li\`o

item.title: Post-transcriptional Regulation of Stochastic Gene Expression Conditioned on Large Deviations
item.description: arXiv:2607.17004v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gene expression is a stochastic process that gives rise to large fluctuations in protein levels leading to phenotypic heterogeneity in clonal cell populations; post-transcriptional regulation plays a crucial role in controlling the level of phenotypic variability within a population, which is directly tied to cell-fate decisions. As such, substantial efforts have been directed towards quantitatively modeling the effects of various post-transcriptional mechanisms on the strength of fluctuations in protein levels (noise). However, the corresponding effects of post-transcriptional regulation on the occurrence of rare events corresponding to large deviations are far less explored and have only been considered for a special model. Here, we take a general model of post-transcriptional regulation and apply the partitioning of Poisson arrivals (PPA) framework to map it onto a model that resembles promoter-based regulation of transcription, leading to a general framework to obtain objects of interest in large deviations (i.e. large deviation rate function for quantifying the likelihood of observing rare protein production rates and the corresponding driven process that characterizes the system dynamics conditional on the rare event) for models of post-transcriptional regulation directly from prior results for promoter-based models. The results derived create new avenues to analyze rare events in general models of post-transcriptional regulation pertaining to various different biological settings.
item.dc:creator: Kenny Wong, Thomas Mourier, Cameron Hopkinson

item.title: Calibeating Prediction-Powered Inference
item.description: arXiv:2604.21260v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study semisupervised mean estimation with a small labeled sample, a large unlabeled sample, and a black-box prediction model whose output may be miscalibrated. A standard approach in this setting is augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) [Robins et al., 1994], which protects against prediction-model misspecification but may be inefficient when the prediction score is poorly aligned with the outcome scale. We introduce Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference, which post-hoc calibrates the prediction score on the labeled sample before using it for semisupervised estimation. This simple step requires no retraining and can calibeat the original score, improving it both as a predictor of the outcome and as a regression adjustment for semisupervised inference. We study both linear and isotonic calibration. For isotonic calibration, we establish first-order optimality guarantees: isotonic post-processing can improve predictive accuracy and estimator efficiency relative to the original score and simpler post-processing rules, while replacing the fitted isotonic score by its conditional-mean oracle yields no additional first-order variance reduction. For linear calibration, we show first-order equivalence to PPI++. We also clarify the relationship between existing estimators, showing that the original PPI estimator is a special case of AIPW and can be inefficient when the prediction model is accurate, while PPI++ is AIPW with empirical efficiency maximization [Rubin and van der Laan, 2008]. In simulations and real-data experiments, our calibrated estimators often outperform PPI and are competitive with, or outperform, AIPW and PPI++. We provide an accompanying Python package, ppi_aipw, at https://larsvanderlaan.github.io/ppi-aipw/.
item.dc:creator: Lars van der Laan, Mark Van Der Laan

item.title: CHRep: Cross-modal Histology Representation and Post-hoc Calibration for Spatial Gene Expression Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2604.21573v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables spatially resolved gene profiling but remains expensive and low-throughput, limiting large-cohort studies and routine clinical use. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides is a promising alternative, yet under realistic leave-one-slide-out evaluation, existing models often suffer from slide-level appearance shifts and regression-driven over-smoothing that suppress biologically meaningful variation. CHRep is a two-phase framework for robust histology-to-expression prediction. In the training phase, CHRep learns a structure-aware representation by jointly optimizing correlation-aware regression, symmetric image-expression alignment, and coordinate-induced spatial topology regularization. In the inference phase, cross-slide robustness is improved without backbone fine-tuning through a lightweight calibration module trained on the training slides, which combines a non-parametric estimate from a training gallery with a magnitude-regularized correction module. Unlike prior embedding-alignment or retrieval-based transfer methods that rely on a single prediction route, CHRep couples topology-preserving representation learning with post-hoc calibration, enabling stable neighborhood retrieval and controlled bias correction under slide-level shifts. Across the three cohorts, CHRep consistently improves gene-wise correlation under leave-one-slide-out evaluation, with the largest gains observed on Alex+10x. Relative to HAGE, the Pearson correlation coefficient on all considered genes [PCC(ACG)] increases by 4.0% on cSCC and 9.8% on HER2+. Relative to mclSTExp, PCC(ACG) further improves by 39.5% on Alex+10x, together with 9.7% and 9.0% reductions in mean squared error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE), respectively.
item.dc:creator: Changfan Wang, Xinran Wang, Donghai Liu, Fei Su, Lulu Sun, Zhicheng Zhao, Zhu Meng

item.title: Flexible Flows for Biological Sequence Design
item.description: arXiv:2606.10543v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Designing functional biological sequences requires navigating vast discrete spaces under strict evolutionary and biophysical constraints. Discrete Flow Matching (DFM) offers a generative framework over such spaces, but existing approaches rely on biologically uninformative couplings and offer limited flexibility for variable-length sequence generation and fine-grained control. We propose a structured coupling that encodes domain-specific preferences among sequence elements, biasing the source distribution toward plausible regions without modifying the flow objective or training procedure. Building on this, we introduce a latent edit-based rate parameterization that models variable-length generation via edit operations conditioned on a shared global latent, akin to a latent variable model, while remaining tractable. We further introduce a latent classifier-free guidance mechanism that steers generation coherently in continuous latent space, along with Dirichlet-prior temperature scaling for test-time control over edit operations. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse biological sequence tasks, including density estimation, unconditional and conditional DNA sequence generation, and peptide sequence generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/FlexFlow.
item.dc:creator: Yogesh Verma, Dani Korpela, Harri L\"ahdesm\"aki, Vikas Garg

item.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Lessons from Biological World Models for Testing Action Effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.01666v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Whether an action-conditioned world model responds to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. Taking biological experiments as the guiding case, we show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model. A second failure arises whenever many sites share one action sequence, as in world models: the pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into an e-value near zero, so a valid test loses its power although the effect is real. Tempering the score changes the bet, not the validity. The log e-value is concave in the tempering factor and zero at zero, so too small a factor costs little and too large a one can cost everything; every single factor we tried, estimated or tuned, failed in some setting, and mixtures over a fixed grid never did. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed by pooling; a tempered statistic, registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field (E = 1.1e10). In three registered tests on models trained by others, the pooled test rejected in 0 of 96 units of a diffusion model, and reached the power bar in 10 of 26 Atari games under IRIS's token likelihood and 1 of 6 control tasks under TD-MPC2; mixtures fixed in advance reached it in 96 units, 24 games and 6 tasks. On recorded robot video with iVideoGPT the mixture rejected in 155 of 159 trajectories; the pooled test did not collapse there (143). Under exact nulls the statistics made 14 rejections in 26,664 tests.
item.dc:creator: Bowen Xu, Boyu Chen, Jiaying Li

item.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)
item.description: arXiv:2611.09429v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite broad potential impact of selection bias it is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct selection bias, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle, applicability, limitations and data requirements. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R and prepares input for the external SPREG software. It provides worked examples using simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with open methodological challenges.
item.dc:creator: Ciarrah-Jane S Barry, Tahereh Gholipourshahraki, Zolt\'an Kutalik, Bjarni J Vilhj\'almsson, Esben Agerbo
